sections.heading: How much jumping the game involves

paragraphs.text: Volleyball is a game of repeated jumps and landings. In video of elite women's matches, each player averaged nearly 22 jump-landings per game. Most jumps were taken off two feet, but more than half of the landings after a block were on one foot. The study covered only two matches among four teams.

support.quote: Videotape recordings of two matches among four volleyball teams were analyzed for this study. Each activity was categorized by jump type (offensive spike or defensive block) ... Each of the players averaged nearly 22 jump-landings per game. Foot use patterns occurred in unequal amounts (p < 0.001) with over 50% of defensive landings occurring on one foot.

paragraphs.text: Setters on one professional team averaged 121 jumps per training session. Sensors on 14 professional players recorded 129,173 jumps across 142 sessions in a season. Weekly totals swung widely, and every player had at least one week in which the jump count doubled.

support.quote: A total of 129 173 jumps were performed during 142 sessions (108 practices, 27 matches, 7 friendly matches). Setters performed the greatest volume of jumps (121 jumps/training session). ... Additionally, each player had at least 1 week with a twofold increase in jumps.

paragraphs.text: In young elite players, more volleyball went with more jumper's knee. A four-year Norwegian study followed 141 players aged 16 to 18, and 28 developed it. Each extra weekly hour of training raised the odds about 1.7 times, and each extra set of matches per week about 3.9 times. Boys had three to four times the risk of girls, and body composition made no difference.

support.quote: We recruited 141 healthy students (69 males and 72 females), and 28 developed jumper's knee (22 boys and six girls). In a multivariate analyses, boys had three to four times higher risk compared with girls. Volleyball training had an odds ratio (OR) 1.72 (1.18-2.53) for every extra hour trained, and match exposure was the strongest sports-related predictor for developing jumper's knee with an OR of 3.88 (1.80-8.40) for every extra set played per week. We did not detect any significant differences between the groups in body composition

paragraphs.text: In adult professional players, a link between jump load and knee pain has not been confirmed. Tracking 65 elite men over three seasons and more than 21,000 sessions, a Norwegian study found no certain link between weekly jump load and knee complaints. Differences in risk were small, and the authors say much larger studies would be needed to settle the question.

support.quote: four men's premier league volleyball teams through three seasons in a prospective cohort study (65 players, 102 player-seasons) ... 21 088 daily player sessions ... No certain evidence of an association was found between weekly jump load and probability of (i) knee complaints ... Small differences in risk across observed jump load levels were observed. It would likely require substantially increased sample sizes to detect this association with certainty.

paragraphs.text: How a player lands may matter for the knee tendon. In a Dutch laboratory study, players who had recovered from jumper's knee landed from drop jumps with stiffer knees and faster loading than healthy players. The authors suggest stiff landing may be a risk factor, though each group had only seven to nine players and the design cannot show cause.

support.quote: (CON, n = 8; PJK, n = 7; RJK, n = 9) ... PJK showed higher knee angular velocities (p<0.01), and higher ankle plantar flexion moment loading rate (p<0.01). ... PJK used a stiffer landing strategy, which may be a risk factor in the development of patellar tendinopathy.

paragraphs.text: Most ACL injuries in volleyball happen without contact, usually when landing from a spike. The ACL is the main ligament in the middle of the knee. A review of 15 studies found the highest rates in female high-school players and in outside hitters, with rates varying widely by exposure and level of play.

support.quote: From an initial pool of 1,491 titles, 15 studies met the inclusion criteria ... substantial variation in ACL injury rates, largely influenced by factors such as exposure time, competition level, and injury mechanism. Notably, non-contact mechanisms were the most frequent cause of ACL injuries, predominantly occurring during spike landings in competitive settings. Female athletes, particularly high school players and those in the outside hitter position, exhibited the highest incidence

paragraphs.text: Shoulder pain is common among competitive volleyball players, though estimates depend on how it is defined. A 2026 review of 27 studies put its prevalence between 22% and 38%. Linked factors included earlier shoulder pain, poor control of the shoulder blade, strength imbalance and the number of arm swings. Most studies were observational and at risk of bias.

support.quote: Twenty-seven studies were included ... Shoulder pain prevalence ranged from 22% (point prevalence) to 38% (lifetime prevalence). ... Reported associated factors included previous shoulder pain or injury, scapular dyskinesis, strength imbalance ... swing volume ... Most evidence was observational, heterogeneous, and at moderate-to-high risk of bias.

paragraphs.text: Hitters and jump servers report more shoulder trouble than other players. Among 422 US college club players, about 60% reported a past shoulder problem, and attackers and jump servers had more problems than setters, defensive players and float servers. Women reported more limitation than men. The study was a one-time survey and examination.

support.quote: A total of 422 athletes returned questionnaires ... Approximately 60% of participants reported a history of shoulder problems. Attackers and "jump" servers were more likely to have shoulder problems than setters, defensive specialists, and "float" servers. ... female athletes providing lower SST scores than male athletes

paragraphs.text: In volleyball, a trial of a shoulder warm-up measured fitness rather than injuries. The eight-week programme improved a shoulder stability test in 32 young elite players. In handball, another overhead sport, a trial in 660 elite players found that shoulder rotation, strength and mobility exercises three times a week in the warm-up lowered the risk of shoulder problems by 28%.

support.quote: Thirty-two healthy young elite male volleyball players ... the "FIFA 11 + shoulder" programme as their warm up protocol, three times per week ... shoulder stability however significantly increased only in the intervention group (p = 0.03

45 elite handball teams (22 female teams, 23 male teams, 660 players) ... an exercise programme to increase glenohumeral internal rotation, external rotation strength and scapular muscle strength, as well as improve kinetic chain and thoracic mobility, was delivered by coaches and captains 3 times per week as a part of the handball warm-up. ... a 28% lower risk of shoulder problems (OR 0.72, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.98, p=0.038)

paragraphs.text: At the top level, volleyball has a low injury rate for a team sport. Data from 32 major international tournaments showed 3.8 time-loss injuries per 1,000 player hours of matches. The ankle accounted for 26% of injuries, the knee 15% and fingers or thumb 11%. The authors note this rate matches studies of lower levels of play.

support.quote: The incidence of time-loss injuries during match play was 3.8/1000 player hours (95% CI 3.0 to 4.5) ... the ankle was the most commonly injured body part (25.9%), followed by the knee (15.2%), fingers/thumb (10.7%) ... which is substantially lower than other major team sports like football ... This injury rate is consistent with previous prospective studies reporting time-loss injuries from lower levels of play

paragraphs.text: One large Dutch trial gives a picture of injury rates in recreational adult play. Among 672 recreational players, the usual-warm-up group had 11.3 acute injuries per 1,000 hours, against 8.9 with a structured warm-up called VolleyVeilig. After adjustment the difference was no longer clear. Injury was counted differently from the elite data, so the two rates cannot be compared directly.

support.quote: The Dutch version of the Oslo Sports Trauma Research Centre questionnaire was used to register and monitor acute and overuse injuries. A total of 672 volleyball players were enrolled ... The incidence rate of acute injury was 21% lower in the intervention group, namely 8.9 versus 11.3 per 1,000 h in the control group (Cox mixed effects crude model: hazard ratio = 0.82 [95%CI: 0.69-0.98]; Cox mixed effects adjusted model: 0.85 [95%CI: 0.71-1.02]).
The incidence of time-loss injuries during match play was 3.8/1000 player hours

paragraphs.text: Blocking is a common source of finger injuries. In a Danish survey of 295 elite and recreational players, indoor injuries occurred mostly during blocking and spiking, with blocking leading to finger injuries. Among Danish elite players, fingers were the most common site of acute injury at 21%, and 28% of all injuries happened while blocking.

support.quote: Injuries in 295 volleyball players were recorded ... Equal numbers of men and women, elite and recreational players were represented. ... In indoor volleyball most injuries occurred during blocking and spiking, resulting most frequently in acute finger and ankle injuries, respectively.
Most injuries occurred in spiking (32%) and in blocking (28%). The injuries were predominantly either acute injuries to fingers (21%) and ankles (18%)

paragraphs.text: A typical finger injury happens when the ball strikes the fingertips at the block. World-level data suggest these injuries are undercounted, because players often tape the finger and keep playing. In Danish emergency department records, women had more hand and finger injuries than men, and the authors called for better blocking and overhand passing technique.

support.quote: a typical situation is during a block where the ball hits the fingertips ... players often continue playing after securing the injured finger with tape

Female players had significantly more hand/finger injuries than male players ... The study suggests the need to enhance prophylactic measures with regard to blocking and overhand pass techniques, in order to reduce the number and extent of ankle and hand/finger injuries.

paragraphs.text: Casual volleyball counts as moderate activity and competitive indoor play as vigorous. The 2024 Compendium of Physical Activities, mostly built on measured values, rates casual team play at 3.0 METs, competitive indoor play at 6.0 and beach play at 8.0. One MET is the energy used sitting quietly. The CDC counts 3 to 5.9 METs as moderate and 6 or more as vigorous.

support.quote: 15711 | 6.0 | Volleyball, competitive, in gymnasium; 15720 | 3.0 | Volleyball, non-competitive, 6 – 9 member team, general; 15725 | 8.0 | Volleyball, beach, in sand
The 2024 Adult Compendium includes 1114 PAs (912 with measured and 202 with estimated values) across 22 Major Headings.

Physical activity that burns 3 to 5.9 METs is moderate intensity. ... Physical activity that burns 6.0 METs or more is vigorous intensity. ... One MET equals the energy or oxygen used while sitting quietly.

paragraphs.text: Much of a volleyball match is played at modest heart rates. In 24 senior female players in Turkey, average heart rate during a match was 117 beats a minute, and every player spent more than half of the match below 60% of her maximum. Liberos had the highest heart rates and setters the lowest.

support.quote: The mean heart rate and blood lactate level of volleyball players were determined 117.2 ± 13.9 bpm ... The setters have the lowest heart rate and the libero players have the highest during the match. All subjects have a heart rate 50-60% and below 50% of their heart rate maximum during more than half of the match duration.

paragraphs.text: Shorter breaks between rallies made the game a better workout in one small trial. In Serbia, 34 untrained men aged 25 to 55 played twice a week for 12 weeks. Both groups lowered their blood pressure, but only the group playing with shorter breaks improved body weight, BMI and a shuttle-run fitness test.

support.quote: Thirty-four healthy untrained men aged 25-55 years were randomized ... Both groups performed volleyball training twice a week over 12 weeks, with participants in MRV playing a modified game with higher intensity due to shorter breaks between rallies. The small to moderate improvements of both groups were observed in SBP ... However, only the MRV significantly improved (p < 0.001) the mean body weight ... and BMI ... and the YYIR1 performance

paragraphs.text: People who play team sports report fewer bad mental health days. In a survey of 1.2 million US adults, those who exercised reported 1.49 fewer poor mental health days a month than matched non-exercisers, and team sports showed the largest difference, at 22%. The survey was a snapshot, so it cannot show that the sport caused the difference.

support.quote: we analysed data from 1 237 194 people aged 18 years or older ... Individuals who exercised had 1·49 (43·2%) fewer days of poor mental health in the past month than individuals who did not exercise but were otherwise matched ... The largest associations were seen for popular team sports (22·3% lower)

paragraphs.text: Reviews of adult sport also link team play with better mental health. A 2023 review of 29 studies linked sport with better wellbeing, less depression, anxiety and stress, and a sense of belonging, with team sport showing more favourable results than individual sport. An earlier review credited the social side of club and team sport, while noting that most studies were cross-sectional.

support.quote: 29 involving adults 18-84 years were included for analysis ... participation in sport (community and elite) is related to better mental health, including improved psychological well-being ... reduced levels of depression, anxiety, and stress ... fostering a sense of belonging ... adults participating in team sport had more favorable health outcomes than those participating in individual sport

club-based or team-based sport seems to be associated with improved health outcomes compared to individual activities, due to the social nature of the participation. ... the capacity to determine the existence and direction of causal links between participation and health is limited by the cross-sectional nature of studies to date.

paragraphs.text: Trials of team sport for mental health are few and mixed. A 2026 review found six studies with 744 adults, with inconsistent effects, and suggested the main value may be wellbeing and social connection. On sticking with exercise, the evidence is indirect: feeling good during exercise and doing it for its own sake are both linked to staying active.

support.quote: Six studies involving 744 participants met the inclusion criteria. ... in non-clinical adult populations, the value of TSG may lie less in producing large reductions in psychiatric symptoms and more in improving psychosocial functioning, perceived well-being, and social connection. ... these effects were inconsistent among studies
24 studies. Feeling better during moderate exercise was linked to future activity; how people felt afterwards was not.
66 studies. Consistent support for a positive relation between more autonomous forms of motivation and exercise.

paragraphs.text: Jump training raises jump height in healthy people. A meta-analysis of 26 studies found that plyometric training, meaning quick rebounding jumps, raised standing jump height by about 9%, and jump height with an arm swing by about 7.5%. On a 50 centimetre jump, 9% would be about 4.5 centimetres.

support.quote: A total of 26 studies ... The pooled estimate of the effect of PT on vertical jump height was 4.7% (95% CI 1.8 to 7.6%), 8.7% (95% CI 7.0 to 10.4%), 7.5% (95% CI 4.2 to 10.8%) and 4.7% (95% CI 0.8 to 8.6%) for the SJ, CMJ, CMJA and DJ, respectively.

paragraphs.text: Jump training programmes of more than 10 weeks and 20 sessions gave the best chance of clear gains. A meta-analysis of 56 studies also found that mixing squat jumps, countermovement jumps and drop jumps beat using one type, and that adding weight brought no extra benefit. People with more sports experience improved more.

support.quote: A meta-analysis of 56 studies ... Subjects with more experience in sport obtained greater enhancements in VJH performance (p < 0.01). ... training volumes of more than 10 weeks and more than 20 sessions, using high-intensity programs (with more than 50 jumps per session), were the strategies that seemed to maximize the probability of obtaining significantly greater improvements ... the combination of different types of plyometrics (squat jump + countermovement jump + drop jump) is recommended rather than using only 1 form ... no extra benefits were found to be gained from doing plyometrics with added weight.

paragraphs.text: Volleyball players gain from jump training even with all the jumping they already do. Across 12 trials in 326 players, plyometric training alone improved jump height, and programme length made no clear difference. Another 2026 review found that splitting the same weekly jumps into more frequent sessions changed little, though certainty was low.

support.quote: 12 controlled trials encompassing a total of 326 volleyball athletes ... standalone plyometric training produced statistically significant improvements in both countermovement jump performance (g = 0.55 ... Subgroup analyses showed no statistically significant between-group differences for CMJ performance by age (Q_between = 3.11, p = 0.077), intervention duration
average differences between higher- and lower-frequency PJT were small when cumulative/average weekly planned volume was matched or closely matched ... Certainty was low for countermovement jump

paragraphs.text: Lifting weights alone may not raise jump height quickly. In a Greek trial of 55 female players over eight weeks, weight training raised squat strength by 17 to 19% in every training group. Jump height improved clearly only in the groups that added drop jumps from a well-chosen height on top of the weights.

support.quote: Fifty-five female volleyball players (age: 23.8 ± 4.3 years) were randomly and equally allocated ... for 8 weeks for a total of 13 sessions. After training, vertical jump performance improved by 3.6-17.4% ( p < 0.05; effect size [ES]: 1.03-1.23) in the OG and the HG compared with the LG, WG, and CG ... Half-squat maximum strength was increased in all experimental groups by 17.4-19% compared with the CG

reviewed.title: A valid and reliable method to measure jump-specific training and competition load in elite volleyball players (Scandinavian Journal of Medicine and Science in Sports, 2018)
reviewed.why_not: Validates a jump-counting device; no health or injury outcome relevant to the reader.

reviewed.title: No effect of eccentric training on jumper's knee in volleyball players during the competitive season: a randomized clinical trial (Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine, 2005)
reviewed.why_not: Holds up, but tendon treatment is covered in the Staying uninjured article; left out to avoid overlap and for length.

reviewed.title: Effectiveness of a warm-up programme to reduce injuries in youth volleyball players: a quasi-experiment (British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2023)
reviewed.why_not: Children aged about 12 to 13 in a non-randomised design; the adult recreational trial of the same programme is cited instead.

reviewed.title: Preventive effect of tailored exercises on patellar tendinopathy in elite youth athletes: A cohort study (Physical Therapy in Sport, 2022)
reviewed.why_not: Non-randomised before-and-after cohort in youth athletes; too weak to support a prevention claim for an adult.

reviewed.title: The impact of warm-up with the volleyveilig approach on upper extremity function in female volleyball players (Scientific Reports, 2025)
reviewed.why_not: 30 players, fitness tests only and no injury outcome.

reviewed.title: The effects of a 16-week periodized linear strength training program incorporating landmine exercises on physical performance in professional female volleyball players (Physical Activity and Nutrition, 2025)
reviewed.why_not: 18 professionals, no untrained control group, and compares an equipment variation rather than strength training itself.

reviewed.title: Heart rate during basketball game play and volleyball drills accurately predicts oxygen uptake and energy expenditure (Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness, 2015)
reviewed.why_not: Develops prediction equations and gives no volleyball intensity figures in the abstract.

reviewed.title: Optimizing position-specific preparation: long-term pre-match warm-up external load analysis using micro-sensor integrated LPS in elite female volleyball players (BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation, 2025)
reviewed.why_not: Warm-up loads in 14 elite players; not informative for recreational play.

reviewed.title: Subjective and Objective Monitoring Markers: Are They Related to Game Performance Indicators in Elite Female Volleyball Players? (International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance, 2024)
reviewed.why_not: About elite performance statistics, not health.

reviewed.title: Ball-Contact Injuries in 11 National Collegiate Athletic Association Sports, 2009-2010 through 2014-2015 (Journal of Athletic Training, 2017)
reviewed.why_not: The abstract does not separate volleyball from the other ten sports.
